facts.statehood_note: President Benjamin Harrison signed the act making Idaho the 43rd state. Idaho had been a territory since 1863.
facts.motto: Esto Perpetua (Latin: "It is perpetuated" or "May it endure forever")
facts.name_origin: Nobody knows for sure. Congress was told "Idaho" was a Shoshone word meaning "gem of the mountains," but later realized the name was possibly made up. A politician named George M. Willing later claimed he invented it after a little girl named Ida.

government.chambers: Idaho Senate (35 senators, one per district) and Idaho House of Representatives (70 representatives, two per district), elected from 35 legislative districts. All 105 members are elected every two years, and they meet each year starting in January at the State Capitol in Boise.
government.executive: Governor (4-year term, no term limits). Other statewide elected officers include the lieutenant governor, secretary of state, state controller, state treasurer, attorney general, and superintendent of public instruction.
government.courts: Idaho Supreme Court (5 justices: a chief justice and four justices). Justices are chosen in nonpartisan elections for 6-year terms; if a seat opens early, the governor appoints from a list made by a judicial nominating commission. The justices choose the chief justice for a 4-year term.
government.local: 44 counties. The five tribal nations in Idaho have their own governments and tribal courts on their lands.
government.constitution: Idaho's first and only constitution was written at a convention that met on July 4, 1889, and voters approved it in November 1889. It has been amended 129 times (as of January 1, 2026).
government.kid_line: "All men are by nature free and equal, and have certain inalienable rights..." (Idaho Constitution, Article I, Section 1)

long_ago.about: The Nimiipuu ("The People") lived in the prairies and river valleys of what is now north Idaho, Montana, Oregon, and Washington, spending winters in sheltered canyon bottomlands. French-Canadian trappers called them "Nez Perce," or "pierced nose."
The Shoshone and Bannock peoples have lived in southern Idaho for more than 10,000 years. Their name for themselves, Newe, means "the people," and the two groups each have their own language.

The Lemhi Shoshone lived in the Lemhi River Valley near present-day Salmon. Sacagawea was born there around 1788, and her brother Cameahwait led the Shoshone band that met Lewis and Clark in August 1805.
The Schitsu'umsh, whose name means "Those who were found here," speak a Salishan language and live in north Idaho. French fur traders gave them the name "Coeur d'Alene."
The Ktunaxa live in far north Idaho near Bonners Ferry. Their language is an isolate, which means it is not related to any other known language.

today.about: Based in Plummer; over 2,500 citizens, a seven-member Tribal Council, and its own Tribal Court; the largest employer in north Idaho.
Based in Bonners Ferry; its council includes a lifetime hereditary chief, and it helps keep alive the only U.S. native source of burbot, a freshwater cod.
Based in Lapwai; over 3,500 citizens led by the nine-member Nez Perce Tribal Executive Committee; its hatchery program helped bring coho salmon back from near extinction.
Based at Fort Hall in southeastern Idaho; over 6,000 citizens, governed by the seven-member Fort Hall Business Council.
About 2,300 citizens on the Duck Valley Reservation, which crosses the Idaho-Nevada border; the tribes guide elk hunts and run trout fisheries.

first_peoples.today_note: Idaho has five federally recognized tribal nations. Each nation's land today is only a small part of its original homeland. The Fort Hall Reservation was set at 1.8 million acres in 1867, then cut to 1.2 million acres in 1872 because of a survey error.
sites: Nez Perce National Historical Park, which tells the Nimiipuu story; its headquarters is at the old Spalding mission site on Lapwai Creek
Weippe Prairie and Canoe Camp near Orofino, where the Nimiipuu helped Lewis and Clark in 1805
Sacajawea Interpretive, Cultural, and Educational Center in Salmon, near Sacagawea's homeland
Bear River Massacre site near Preston, where at least 250 Shoshone people were killed in 1863

history.event: Paleo-Indian big-game hunters (the Clovis, Folsom, and Plano cultures) live in Idaho. Mammoths roam the land.
In the Archaic period, people build homes partly underground and gather and process more plants for food.
Indigenous Peoples use bows and arrows and pottery; later, horses brought west by the Spanish change travel and hunting.

Lewis and Clark enter Idaho at Lemhi Pass. Sacagawea (Lemhi Shoshone) finds her brother Cameahwait, and the Nimiipuu (Nez Perce) give food, canoe help, and directions at Weippe Prairie. York, a Black man enslaved by William Clark, is part of the expedition.
Fort Henry, the first American-owned fur trading post west of the Rocky Mountains, is built near St. Anthony.
Fur trading posts Fort Hall and Fort Boise are built. Boise later takes its name from the old fort.
Henry and Eliza Spalding start a mission and school among the Nimiipuu on Lapwai Creek.
Treaties between the United States and the Nimiipuu divide Nez Perce families and take land, leading to anger over lost land and attacks that go unpunished.

Franklin, Idaho's first town, is founded in 1860, and big gold strikes bring miners to the Clearwater, Salmon River, and Boise Basin areas. Mexican miners work near Rocky Bar, and by 1870 most of Idaho's miners are Chinese.

On January 29, about 200 U.S. soldiers led by Colonel Patrick Connor attack a Shoshone camp on the Bear River near present-day Preston, killing at least 250 Shoshone people (the Bear River Massacre). In March, Congress creates Idaho Territory, with Lewiston as its first capital.
During the Civil War, Idaho's volunteer soldiers do not fight the Confederacy; they guard Oregon Trail travelers and the routes connecting East and West.
After a heated political fight, the territorial capital moves from Lewiston to Boise.
A presidential order creates the Fort Hall Reservation for the Shoshone and Bannock at 1.8 million acres; a survey error cuts it to 1.2 million acres in 1872.

The Nez Perce War begins with a Nimiipuu victory at White Bird Canyon in June. Soldiers chase Chief Joseph's people and other bands about 1,100 miles until the war ends at Bear Paw, Montana, in October, about 40 miles from Canada.
Idaho writes its constitution in 1889, and on July 3, 1890, Idaho becomes the 43rd state.

trailblazers.name: Sacagawea
trailblazers.years: c. 1788 to 1812 (some accounts say much later)
trailblazers.text: Sacagawea was born around 1788, likely in the Lemhi River Valley near Salmon, and was captured by Hidatsa raiders as a child. On the Lewis and Clark Expedition she saved records from a capsized boat, found camas roots for food, and in 1805 was reunited with her brother Cameahwait, a Shoshone leader. Clark wrote that a woman traveling with the men was "a token of peace."

trailblazers.name: York
trailblazers.text: York was a Black man enslaved by William Clark who traveled with the Lewis and Clark Expedition. He was part of the 1805 group that became the first Euro-American expedition to enter what is now Idaho, crossing at Lemhi Pass and meeting the Shoshone and Nimiipuu peoples.

trailblazers.name: Jesús Urquides
trailblazers.text: Born in Sonora, Mexico, Jesús Urquides ran mule pack trains that carried supplies to mines across six western states. He settled in Boise in the late 1860s, moved 10,000 pounds of cable 70 miles to the Yellow Jacket Mine with a 35-mule train, and built about 30 cabins for his mostly Mexican-born workers, a neighborhood called Urquides' Spanish Village.

trailblazers.name: Polly Bemis (Lalu Nathoy)
trailblazers.text: Born near Beijing, China, Polly was sold as a young woman and brought to the mining town of Warren, Idaho, in 1872. She married Charles Bemis in 1894, and they farmed fruit and vegetables on the Salmon River and sold extra food to river travelers. Her restored log cabin opened as a museum in 1987.

trailblazers.name: Emma Edwards Green
trailblazers.text: Emma Edwards Green designed Idaho's state seal, which the legislature adopted on March 14, 1891. It is the only state seal in the country designed by a woman, and it shows the motto Esto Perpetua.

trailblazers.name: Moses Alexander
trailblazers.text: Moses Alexander was elected governor of Idaho in 1914 and re-elected in 1916. He was Idaho's first Jewish governor.

trailblazers.name: Larry EchoHawk
trailblazers.text: In 1990, Larry EchoHawk was elected Idaho's attorney general. He was the first Native American elected attorney general of any U.S. state.

landforms: Rocky Mountains, including the Lost River Range
Borah Peak (Mt. Borah), the highest point at 12,662 feet
Hells Canyon, the deepest gorge in the United States
Bitterroot Mountains and Lemhi Pass on the Montana border
waters: Snake River (lowest point, 770 feet, at Lewiston)
Lake Pend Oreille, the largest lake (180 square miles)
Coeur d'Alene, St. Joe, St. Maries, and Kootenai rivers
geography.regions: Idaho has the narrow, forested Panhandle in the north, high mountains through the middle, and the Snake River Plain across the south, where most people live and farm.

ecosystems.name: Sagebrush high desert
ecosystems.about: Southern Idaho's dry high desert is covered with sagebrush, rabbitbrush, and grasses, and sandhill cranes fly along the Snake River.

ecosystems.name: Spring-fed wetlands
ecosystems.about: Springs along the Snake River near Hagerman stay the same temperature all year, so wetlands do not freeze and many migrating waterfowl spend the winter there; the steady water is also good for raising trout.

ecosystems.name: Northern rivers and lakes
ecosystems.about: North Idaho has more than 2,000 lakes and big rivers; the Kootenai Tribe helps keep the only U.S. native source of burbot (a freshwater cod), and the Nez Perce Tribe helped bring coho salmon back from near extinction.

ecosystems.name: Mountain forests
ecosystems.about: The U.S. Forest Service manages about 38% of Idaho's land, more than in any other state, and the western white pine is the state tree.

science.weather: Idaho's weather changes a lot from place to place. The state record high is 118°F at Orofino (1934) and the record low is -60°F at Island Park Dam (1943). Southern Idaho is dry high desert.
science.resources: Idaho grows about one-third of the nation's potatoes and is a leading trout producer. Timber, silver and other mining, food processing, and tourism are also important, and the state has about 72 kinds of precious and semi-precious stones.
science.highlight: Hagerman Fossil Beds: the Hagerman horse (Equus simplicidens), Idaho's state fossil, lived about 4 to 3 million years ago and is the earliest-known single-toed horse. Remains of over 200 horses were found, and Smithsonian digs in the 1930s found about 120 skulls and 20 complete skeletons.
